newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ seeks to soothe markets on rate comment report.
newsitem.headline: BOJ seeks to soothe markets on rate comment report.

text.p: Tokyo share prices sank, Japanese government bonds slid and the dollar dipped on Wednesday after Bank of Japan Deputy Governor Toshihiko Fukui was quoted as saying the central bank was considering the right timing to tighten credit.
But another central bank official said later that Fukui had been misquoted and that the Bank of Japan had not changed its monetary stance and had no plans for an immediate rate rise.
Many economists insisted that an early rate rise remained unlikely given economic uncertainties, the yen's recent rise and worries over Japan's financial sector.

Fukui was quoted by an executive of a labour group as saying the central bank was considering the right timing to raise its official discount rate, at which it lends to commercial banks, but did not want to make a hasty decision.

The comment, revealed after Fukui's meeting with executives of Japan's largest grouping of labour unions, the Japanese Trade Union Confederation (Rengo), triggered massive selling of Japanese government bond futures and cash bonds, traders said.
Rengo at the meeting urged the central bank to raise the key rate, now at a record low 0.5 percent.

Ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) officials have also been calling for higher rates out of fear that a liberalisation of Japan's foreign exchange laws in April 1998 will trigger a massive outflow of capital from Japan.
A senior BOJ official, however, told reporters Wednesday evening in a hastily called press briefing that the central bank had had no change in policy.

The Tokyo stock market's key index, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares, already undermined by worries over the strong yen, closed down 490.85 points at 19,841.98 after earlier tumbling more than 500 points.

"The BOJ comment came at a time when the market was on edge about a rate raise, due to recent media reports that the LDP was in favour of a rate hike, and it startled both foreign and domestic investors into selling," said Hisao Suzuki at Yamaichi Securities.

The dollar dipped briefly against the yen on the comments, which fanned speculation that the central bank would be willing to raise its rock-bottom interest rates sooner rather than later. It eased from highs above 114 yen to stand around 114.14 yen in late Tokyo trade, but this was still well above its level in late New York on Tuesday of under 113 yen.
The Bank of Japan cut the discount rate to a record low 0.5 percent in September 1995 to keep the economy from faltering.
But speculation that the central bank wants to tighten credit in view of the economy's recovery has been growing amid calls for higher rates from some ruling party politicians.
Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita said earlier on Wednesday that the bank's low interest rate policy was revitalising the economy and benefiting the people.
He added that a recent rise in Japan's long-term interest rates reflected confidence in the nation's economic outlook.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, meanwhile, urged politicians not to comment on interest rates and said he did not think LDP officials wanted to ask for a rate rise.
Several economists said the central bank was not ready to raise the discount rate soon, though some predicted it would let short-term rates rise earlier, perhaps during the summer.

"Markets will realise the economy is not doing so well in the April-June period and realise they will have to wait until the next 'tankan' survey expected out in July. Then they will settle down," said Yasuhiko Ushikubo, an economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan. The "tankan" is a quarterly survey by the central bank of corporate sentiment.
